findings.title: Silent failure: withdraw confirmation silently dropped when insufficient gas balance
findings.description: When RemoteAssetAdapter handles a withdrawal command from Hub, it updates local state (reduces protocolDeposits and totalDeposited) then attempts to send a confirmation back to Hub. If the contract lacks sufficient native balance for LayerZero fees, the confirmation is SILENTLY SKIPPED -- no revert, no error event, no logging. The Hub's CrossChainAssetController already optimistically decremented its deployedAssets/totalDeployed tracking. If the withdrawal actually failed on the DeFi protocol side (which this simplified version doesn't even attempt), the Hub would have permanently incorrect accounting with no way to detect the discrepancy. This is a fund-safety critical silent failure in cross-chain message handling.
findings.suggestion: Either (1) revert the entire _handleWithdraw if confirmation cannot be sent, so the LZ message fails and can be retried, or (2) emit a ConfirmationFailed event with the amount so monitoring can detect the gap, or (3) store unconfirmed withdrawals in a queue and provide a retryConfirmation() function. Option 1 is safest: `require(address(this).balance >= fee.nativeFee, 'InsufficientGasForConfirmation');`

findings.title: Silent failure: yield report silently dropped when insufficient gas balance
findings.description: Same pattern as ERR-001 but for yield reports. When _handleHarvest is called and yield is calculated, the yield report to Hub is silently dropped if the contract has insufficient native balance. The Hub never receives the yield data. No event is emitted to indicate the report was not sent. This creates invisible accounting gaps in the cross-chain yield tracking system.
findings.suggestion: Revert the transaction if the yield report cannot be sent: `if (address(this).balance < fee.nativeFee) revert InsufficientFeeForReport();`. Alternatively, store the yield amount in a pending state and provide a manual retry mechanism.

findings.title: Silent skip: MSG_MINT_SHARES silently ignores invalid receiver or zero shares
findings.description: When the Hub sends a MSG_MINT_SHARES cross-chain message to confirm a deposit, if receiver is address(0) or shares is 0, the mint is silently skipped. No revert, no event. The Hub believes shares were minted to the user, but nothing happened. The user deposited real assets (transferred in the deposit() call) but receives zero shares. This is a direct fund loss scenario where a corrupted or malicious cross-chain message causes user deposits to vanish silently.
findings.suggestion: Revert on invalid receiver or zero shares so the LayerZero message is marked as failed and can be retried: `if (receiver == address(0)) revert ZeroAddress(); if (shares == 0) revert InvalidAmount(); pptOft.mint(receiver, shares);`. This ensures the Hub can detect and retry the operation.

findings.title: Encoding/decoding mismatch in CreditManager cross-chain messages
findings.description: sendCredits() encodes the payload as `abi.encode(MSG_SEND_CREDIT, amount)` which ABI-encodes a bytes1 value as a full 32-byte word (left-padded). The first byte of the encoded payload will be 0x00 (padding), NOT 0x01 (MSG_SEND_CREDIT). On the receiving side, `_lzReceive` reads `bytes1(payload[0])` which will be 0x00, not the intended message type. Similarly, `abi.decode(payload[1:], (uint256))` will fail because it starts at offset 1 instead of 32. The satellite-side receiver (which would decode these messages) will also have this mismatch. The sendCredits path from Hub currently sends via abi.encode but any receiver using the bytes1 extraction pattern will fail to decode correctly.
findings.suggestion: Use `abi.encodePacked(MSG_SEND_CREDIT, abi.encode(amount))` for encoding (matching the pattern used in PPTSatellite._buildDepositPayload), so that the first byte is literally the message type. Alternatively, use `abi.encode` consistently and decode as `(bytes1 msgType, uint256 amount) = abi.decode(payload, (bytes1, uint256))` on the receiver side.

findings.title: CrossChainAssetController: optimistic state update with no rollback mechanism on remote failure
findings.description: withdrawFromRemote() optimistically decrements deployedAssets, protocolAllocations, and totalDeployed BEFORE the remote chain confirms the withdrawal. If the remote chain's _handleWithdraw reverts (e.g., ProtocolNotSupported, InsufficientDeposit), the LZ message delivery fails but the Hub has already decremented its tracking. There is no mechanism to rollback the optimistic decrement. The comment acknowledges this ('optimistic update - will be confirmed by remote') but the confirmation handler (MSG_WITHDRAW_CONFIRM in _lzReceive) only emits an event without any state reconciliation. This leads to permanently incorrect accounting.
findings.suggestion: Implement a pending withdrawal pattern: (1) store the withdrawal in a pending map keyed by a nonce/guid, (2) only decrement tracking when MSG_WITHDRAW_CONFIRM is received, (3) add a timeout/expiry mechanism to handle cases where confirmation never arrives. Alternatively, only decrement tracking in the _lzReceive handler when MSG_WITHDRAW_CONFIRM is received.

findings.title: PPTOFT._lzReceive lacks ReentrancyGuard protection
findings.description: Unlike PPTOFTAdapter (which uses nonReentrant), CrossChainAssetController (nonReentrant), and RemoteAssetAdapter (nonReentrant), PPTOFT._lzReceive does not use ReentrancyGuard. While _mint() itself is not externally exploitable in a standard ERC20, if PPTOFT is ever extended with hooks (ERC777-style) or if the recipient is a contract with a receive hook, reentrancy through the minting path could be exploited. Given this is a cross-chain fund handling contract, defense-in-depth requires consistent reentrancy protection.
findings.suggestion: Add ReentrancyGuard to PPTOFT and apply `nonReentrant` modifier to `_lzReceive`. All other cross-chain receive handlers in this codebase already follow this pattern.

findings.title: PPTOFTAdapter: approve() used instead of safeIncreaseAllowance, no allowance reset
findings.description: In _handleRedemption, the code first calls `approve(redemptionManager, shares)` then immediately calls `safeTransfer(redemptionManager, shares)`. The approve is never consumed since safeTransfer is used (which doesn't use allowance). This means redemptionManager retains an outstanding allowance equal to `shares` that it could use to drain tokens later. Additionally, some tokens (like USDT) require allowance to be set to 0 before setting a new value. The same pattern exists in _handleDeposit (line 346) with vault.
findings.suggestion: If the intention is to let redemptionManager pull tokens, use only approve() and then call the manager's function that uses transferFrom. If the intention is to push tokens, use only safeTransfer() and remove the approve. Also consider using `forceApprove()` from SafeERC20 for non-standard tokens.

findings.title: PPTOFTAdapter._requestRedemption: generates pseudo-random requestId instead of calling actual RedemptionManager
findings.description: This is labeled as a placeholder/non-production implementation but is part of the codebase with no guard preventing deployment. The function transfers real tokens to redemptionManager but generates a fake requestId from a hash instead of calling the actual RedemptionManager contract. If deployed as-is, tokens are transferred but no actual redemption request is created. Users would lose their shares with no way to complete the redemption. The virtual modifier allows override, but the base implementation is dangerous.
findings.suggestion: Either implement the actual RedemptionManager call or add a revert to prevent this placeholder from being used in production: `revert('NOT_IMPLEMENTED');`. Mark the function as abstract if possible, or add a deployment check that verifies the override is in place.

findings.title: RemoteAssetAdapter._handleDeploy: updates tracking without actually deploying assets to the protocol
findings.description: The _handleDeploy function receives a cross-chain command to deploy assets to a DeFi protocol (Aave, Compound, etc.) but only updates accounting variables without actually performing any token transfer or protocol interaction. The Hub's CrossChainAssetController has already incremented its deployedAssets tracking. If deployed as-is, the Hub thinks assets are deployed and earning yield, but tokens remain idle in the adapter contract (or may not even be present). Combined with _calculateYield always returning 0, this creates a complete disconnect between Hub accounting and reality.
findings.suggestion: Implement the actual protocol deposit call or revert with a clear error indicating the function is not yet implemented. At minimum, verify the contract holds sufficient asset balance before updating tracking: `require(asset.balanceOf(address(this)) >= amount, 'InsufficientBalance');`

findings.title: PPTSatellite.deposit routes user deposits to LiquidityPool which has no LP accounting
findings.description: PPTSatellite.deposit() takes user assets and calls liquidityPool.addLiquidity(). However, LiquidityPool.addLiquidity() is a public function with no caller restrictions and no LP share tracking. It only transfers tokens in and emits LiquidityAdded. Meanwhile, LiquidityPool.removeLiquidity() is also public and allows anyone to withdraw tokens up to the pool balance. This means: (1) deposited user funds can be drained by anyone calling removeLiquidity(), (2) there is no way to distinguish user deposit funds from LP-provided liquidity, (3) the credit system tracks utilization but actual fund custody is unprotected.
findings.suggestion: Either (1) restrict addLiquidity/removeLiquidity to authorized addresses (onlyOwner or a whitelist), or (2) implement LP share accounting (mint LP tokens on addLiquidity, burn on removeLiquidity), or (3) have PPTSatellite transfer assets directly to the pool without going through the public addLiquidity function.

findings.title: CreditManager.rebalance: fee distribution can leave chains without sufficient fee
findings.description: The rebalance function divides msg.value equally across chains. However, different chains may have different LayerZero fees. If chain A requires 0.01 BNB and chain B requires 0.05 BNB, splitting 0.06 BNB equally (0.03 each) would cause chain B's _lzSend to revert with insufficient fee. The last chain gets the remainder, but intermediate chains get the fixed feePerChain which may be insufficient. Additionally, if some chains only need credit reduction (no message sent), they still consume their share of the fee, leaving less for chains that need messages.
findings.suggestion: Either (1) accept per-chain fees as a parameter array, (2) quote each chain's fee using _quote() before sending and validate total msg.value covers all, or (3) skip fee allocation for chains that only decrease credit (no _lzSend needed for local-only operations).

findings.title: CreditManager._payNative: cumulative fee validation insufficient for multi-send
findings.description: The _payNative override is intended to support multiple _lzSend calls in the rebalance function. However, it only checks `msg.value < _nativeFee` against the individual send fee, not the cumulative total. Since msg.value remains constant across all calls within the same transaction, this check passes for each individual send as long as msg.value >= the single largest fee, even if the total fees exceed msg.value. This allows the contract to 'pay' more in total fees than was actually sent, effectively spending ETH/BNB that belongs to the contract.
findings.suggestion: Track cumulative fees spent in a transient storage variable or a local accumulator, and validate that the total does not exceed msg.value. Example: add a state variable `uint256 private _totalFeesPaid;` that accumulates in _payNative and is checked/reset in rebalance.

findings.title: DeltaLib.calculateOptimalWeights: rounding error causes weights to not sum to BPS_DENOMINATOR
findings.description: When totalUsage is 0, equal weights are calculated as `10000 / N`. For N=3 chains, each gets 3333, totaling 9999 (missing 1 BPS). For N=7, each gets 1428, totaling 9996 (missing 4 BPS). The same rounding issue applies to the non-zero branch where individual weight calculations via integer division lose precision. The validateWeights function would return false for these outputs, but calculateOptimalWeights itself doesn't validate its own output. Any caller using these weights for credit allocation will under-allocate credits.
findings.suggestion: Assign the remainder to the last element: `weights[usages.length - 1] += BPS_DENOMINATOR - (equalWeight * usages.length);`. Apply the same fix in the non-zero totalUsage branch.

findings.title: PPTOFTAdapter._handleDeposit: ERC4626 deposit may return fewer shares than expected with no slippage check
findings.code_snippet:
// Call vault deposit
uint256 shares = IERC4626(vault).deposit(assets, receiver);
findings.description: The cross-chain deposit handler calls IERC4626(vault).deposit() without any minimum shares check. The user on the satellite chain specified a deposit amount, but by the time the cross-chain message arrives and is processed, the vault's share price may have changed unfavorably (e.g., due to NAV update or donation attack). The user has no way to cancel the deposit since their assets were already taken on the satellite chain. There is no slippage protection for the user in this cross-chain deposit path.
findings.suggestion: Include a minShares parameter in the cross-chain deposit message (from PPTSatellite.deposit). In _handleDeposit, verify `shares >= minShares` after the vault deposit call, reverting if slippage is exceeded. This allows the LZ message to be retried when conditions are more favorable.

summary.verdict: FAIL - Critical silent failures in cross-chain message handling. Three P0 findings: RemoteAssetAdapter silently drops withdrawal confirmations and yield reports when gas is insufficient (ERR-001, ERR-002), and PPTSatellite silently skips share minting on invalid parameters (ERR-003). Seven P1 findings cover encoding mismatches that would cause message decode failures (ERR-004), optimistic state updates without rollback (ERR-005), missing reentrancy protection (ERR-006), dangling approvals (ERR-007), placeholder production code (ERR-008, ERR-009), and unprotected fund custody (ERR-010). These findings represent systemic risk in a cross-chain fund transfer system where silent failures can directly cause loss of user funds.
